contributions: Reasoning Jury: a two-phase panel judge in which jurors first judge a step-segmented trace independently and are then combined by either a consolidation pass or a moderated multi-turn deliberation, producing a single deduplicated verdict grounding each defect in [STEP-k] locations with a description, severity and evidence.
A moderator design that is blind to the problem, trace and candidate solution, so its speaker selection and termination decisions are necessarily about argument dynamics rather than content.
Evidence that juries of cheap open-weight models exceed frontier single judges at step-level defect localization (80.2-82.3 vs 73.7 for opus-4.6 on Hard2Verify) and that the gain is driven by recall.
A cost analysis showing the jury uses 7.6x the tokens and 10.9x the calls of a single frontier judge while costing 6.4x less in dollars, and 12x less in consolidation mode.

A diversity control showing that a homogeneous jury of three independent samples of one model captures most of the lift (+13.0 for gpt-oss-120b), so model diversity is not necessary though base-model capability caps the result.
Ablations on jury size, moderator choice, and simpler aggregators (majority vote, union of defects) that localize where the gain comes from.
A task-based test that the diagnosis and severity fields carry value beyond step localization: defect-guided retry reaches 76.2% vs 71.2% on flagged traces (McNemar p = 4e-5).
datasets: Hard2Verify (200 human-annotated step-level records, advanced math competitions)
AIME2026 (30 problems, used for profiling and defect-guided retry)
ProcessBench (discussed and deliberately not used, traces too short)
limitations: Stated: deliberation is sequential with an unknown number of turns, so it adds wall-clock latency that rules out on-policy RL though it is tolerable off-policy and for offline curation; it uses 7.6x the tokens and 10.9x the LLM calls of a single judge, which binds wherever throughput or rate limits, rather than dollars, are the constraint; the benchmark scoring validates only step localization, not explanation factuality, severity calibration, evidence quality or semantic deduplication; the jury's defect fingerprints are the jury's own judgements rather than ground truth, the demonstration taxonomy is one induction run at non-zero temperature and is explicitly not offered as a standard, and per-step rates are confounded by how finely the segmenter splits a trace; the moderator's trace-blindness is a heuristic whose causal effect was not isolated. Points a reader should notice: (a) Hard2Verify is 200 records with CIs of +-2.5 to +-3.1, so the deliberation-over-consolidation gap of 0.4-1.5 points is not resolvable and should not be read as a real ordering; (b) the paper's own union-of-defects baseline beats deliberation in two of six panels, which undercuts the deliberation machinery as the source of the accuracy gain even as the authors defend it on output-structure grounds; (c) the cost comparison prices open-weight models at Bedrock list rates as of one month while the models were actually served on a local vLLM cluster, so it compares an API bill to a hypothetical one and excludes serving cost and the latency the paper elsewhere admits matters; (d) the paper's own prompt scores 83.9 against the 85.3 they replicate with the Hard2Verify prompt on the same model, so the prompt was adopted for its extra fields at a small accuracy cost; (e) profiling and retry rest on a single generator (nemotron-3-super) on a single 30-problem benchmark; (f) the retry evaluation compares rich feedback against step anchors only, never against no feedback or against plain resampling at matched compute.
method: The trace is first segmented into referenceable steps. Rather than the usual double-newline split (which breaks code blocks, multi-line derivations and case enumerations) or LLM re-segmentation (unstable across samples and unfaithful to the original text), they use the regex (?<=[.!?])\s*\n\s*\n+ so a boundary requires an end-of-sentence character. Phase 1: every juror gets the same prompt with the problem, the step-annotated trace and the final solution, and independently returns JSON verdicts, each with what_went_wrong, statement_refs (the [STEP-k] locations), impact (neutral/minor/major/fatal) and evidence. The prompt enforces a genericness test ('could this comment apply to a different problem with no edits? if so, rewrite it') and a 1-5 specificity self-check keeping only issues scoring >= 4. Phase 1 calls fan out in parallel. Phase 2 has two modes. Consolidation is one extra judge call that sees all Phase 1 verdicts and verifies, merges and fills gaps, emitting the Phase 1 schema. Deliberation is multi-turn: the moderator is deliberately blind to the problem, the trace and the candidate solution and sees only the deliberation transcript, so its role is purely procedural — pick the next speaker, prioritize jurors in unresolved disagreements, recall anyone silent two or more turns, fold contributions into a running consensus state, detect termination (a full round with no new argument, universal agreement, cycling, or a hard turn cap). The authors' stated reason for the blindness is that a moderator who could see the trace would form opinions and become a covert extra juror able to suppress dissent by never giving it the floor; they call this a design heuristic whose causal effect they did not isolate. A final extraction call synthesizes consensus defects (endorsed by a dynamically computed majority of the jurors that actually succeeded, or raised and never contested), a confidence in [0,1], dissenting views, and the termination reason.
methods: Reasoning Jury (Phase 1 independent judgement, Phase 2 consolidation or deliberation)
genericness test and 1-5 specificity self-check in the juror prompt
majority vote and union-of-defects aggregation baselines
Balanced F1 at step level, bootstrap CIs, exact McNemar test
gpt-oss-120b, glm-5.2, deepseek-v4-pro, kimi-k2.6, nemotron-3-super, minimax-m3, minimax-m2.7, qwen3.6-27b, gemma-4-31b
one_liner: Replaces the single LLM judge of a long reasoning trace with a panel of jurors that first judge independently and then reach consensus through a blind moderator's deliberation or a consolidation pass, letting cheap open-weight models beat frontier single judges at step-level defect localization for a fraction of the dollar cost.
problem: Curating SFT data, giving RL a reward signal, and doing error analysis on reasoning models all require deciding not just whether the final answer is right but which step went wrong and how badly. Long chains of thought have tens to hundreds of interdependent steps where one bad step propagates, and single-model judges, including frontier models, do this poorly. Separately, terms of use generally forbid using closed-weight frontier models to train other LLMs, so a high-fidelity judge built only from open-weight models is a practical necessity rather than a preference.

relevance.overthinking: Largely tangential. The paper is about how to evaluate a reasoning trace for defects, not about how long a model should reason; it never measures reasoning length as an outcome, has no accuracy-versus-token-budget curve for the model under study, and the keyword match ('reasoning trace') is generic. Token efficiency appears once in the introduction as a dimension such feedback might eventually improve, and is not measured. Two things are still worth carrying over. First, its exploratory defect profile of nemotron-3-super on AIME2026 finds that the largest and almost entirely fatal defect leaf is 'extended reasoning on an uncorrected false premise' — a failure of not stopping or backtracking, which is the mechanism behind wasted reasoning stated as a defect category rather than as a token count, and it is measured on 1,920 traces averaging 13,025 tokens. It also reports 0.99 defects per trace even when the final answer is correct, which is a caution against using final-answer correctness as the label for whether a trace's length was justified. Second, and separately from the reasoning topic itself, it is a data point on spending test-time compute on the evaluator: 7.6x tokens and 10.9x calls across a deliberating panel of small open models beat a single frontier judge and cost 6.4x less, which is the same compute-allocation question the group tracks, moved from the solver to the judge. The paper's own union-of-defects baseline suggests most of that gain comes from pooling independent samples rather than from the extra deliberation turns.

results: Scoring converts the rich verdicts into a step-level binary signal (a step referenced at minor or above is 1) against the benchmarks' own gold boundaries, so the benchmark numbers evaluate localization only and say nothing about explanation factuality, severity calibration, evidence or dissent. Hard2Verify (200 records, ~780 gold error steps, ~9.3 steps per record of which ~3.9 erroneous), all calls at reasoning effort High and temperature 1.0, 95% bootstrap CIs over 10,000 record-level resamples. Single judges: gpt-5.4 83.9 Balanced F1 is a saturated outlier ten points clear of opus-4.6 at 73.7 (precision 81.7 but recall only 62.5), then sonnet-4.6 71.2, gemini-3.1-pro 69.5, glm-5.2 69.4, with open-weight models spanning ~50-70. Juries (deliberation / consolidation): Frontier 84.4 / 83.2, Frontier minus gpt-5.4 81.7 / 81.3, Large OSS 80.2 / 78.8, Small-Medium OSS 80.8 / 79.3. The pattern is that when one juror saturates the task consensus just tracks that juror (Frontier adds 0.5 over gpt-5.4 alone), and when none does, pooling gives large gains driven by recall: the OSS juries beat their best member by 10.8 and 15.4 points and beat opus-4.6, sonnet-4.6 and gemini-3.1-pro by 7.1-11.3. Deliberation beats consolidation by 0.4-1.5 points, a difference within the +-2.5 to +-3.1 CIs, and the real distinction is a precision-recall trade: deliberation raises recall (71.3 to 75.0 and 71.3 to 77.4) while consolidation raises precision (79.6 to 81.1 and 78.3 to 82.9). Ablations: jury size can drop to three jurors within 1.3 points for Frontier, Frontier-minus-gpt-5.4 and Large OSS (Frontier is flat from five to two, 84.4 to 84.7, because gpt-5.4 carries the verdict), while Small-Medium OSS holds through four (-1.1) but loses 4.0 at three. Moderator choice moves consensus 2.6-3.7 points under deliberation and 6.1-6.4 under consolidation. Diversity is not required: a homogeneous jury of three temperature-1.0 samples of gpt-oss-120b with a same-model moderator reaches 82.3 (+13.0 over solo) and 3x qwen3.6-27b reaches 72.5 (+11.8), so independent sampling alone produces most of the lift, but the ceiling tracks base-model strength. DeltaBench (1,226 records) reproduces the pattern at a lower level: 3x gpt-oss-120b jury 61.5 vs opus-4.6 58.4 and gpt-5.4 61.8, individual jurors 53.3-55.7, lift +5.8; under DeltaBench's own macro-F1 protocol 47.9 vs 43.4. Against simpler aggregation, majority voting collapses recall to 38-63% (precision 86-93%) and sits 9-26 points below consensus, but a plain union of defects is competitive — deliberation beats it in only four of six panels — so the authors concede the accuracy gain comes mainly from pooling independent judgements, with consolidation/deliberation contributing adjudication, deduplication and structure rather than step-level score. Cost on the same 200 records: single opus-4.6 is 4.2M tokens, 200 calls, $79.13, 73.7 Balanced F1; the 3x gpt-oss jury under deliberation is 31.9M tokens (7.6x) and 2,173 calls (10.9x) yet $12.35 (6.4x cheaper) at 82.3, and under consolidation 14.3M tokens, 800 calls, $6.50 (12x cheaper) at 80.3, because gpt-oss-120b output is priced at $0.62/M against opus-4.6's $25/M. Profiling (exploratory, jury verdicts not validated as ground truth): over 1,920 nemotron-3-super AIME2026 traces (295,453 steps, 84.6 tokens per step, 13,025 tokens per trace) the jury flags 8,711 steps — 3,681 fatal, 3,270 major, 1,703 minor, 57 neutral — and within self-monitoring and error-handling the single largest and almost entirely fatal taxonomy leaf is 'extended reasoning on an uncorrected false premise'. Defect counts track answer correctness: 0.99 defects per correct-answer trace (0.17 fatal) versus 4.86 per wrong-answer trace (2.31 fatal), roughly 5x overall and 14x on fatal, while the correct-answer rate being non-zero exposes right-answer-flawed-reasoning traces. Defect-guided retry on those traces: 877 of 1,920 (45.7%) carry a non-neutral defect, capturing 372 of the 384 wrong answers (96.9% recall); retrying with step locations plus the what_went_wrong diagnosis and severity gives 668/877 (76.2%) against 624/877 (71.2%) with locations alone, repairing more wrong answers (181 vs 146) and regressing fewer correct ones (18 vs 27), lifting corpus accuracy from 80.0% to 88.5% vs 86.2%, with exact McNemar p = 4e-5 and a problem-level advantage of +4.1pp (bootstrap 95% CI [+2.3, +6.1], better on 15 of 29 problems, worse on 1).
